meta.case_name: Two Jars of Wine – Brain Teaser

prompt.context: Picture a small town with a population of 10,000 people in rural Austria. A river divides the town. There is only one bridge with two lanes over this river and this is the only crossing point for several hundreds of kilometers. A factory stands on one side of the river and the entire population lives on the other side of the river.
prompt.question: The mayor of the village approaches you and tells you that the bridge presents a bottleneck to the village during rush hour when people are going to work (i.e. there are severe traffic jams). He wants you to solve the problem without spending a lot of money. What solutions would you recommend?

clarifying_info.q: All villagers live on one side of the river and only the factory stands on the other side?
clarifying_info.a: Correct. All villagers live on the right-hand side of the river and only the factory stands on the left-hand side. Only the villagers from the right-hand side work in this factory.

clarifying_info.q: Is it possible to build another bridge?
clarifying_info.a: No. We want to keep this as cheap as possible.

clarifying_info.q: What time do the villagers go to work?
clarifying_info.a: There are two shifts; the first begins at 8am and the second starts at 9am. Each worker works 8 hours. Then they go home.

clarifying_info.q: Do all men and women work at the factory?
Does anyone besides the men have a reason to cross the bridge?

framework: Clarify the physical setup (one bridge, two lanes, all workers on one side)
Quantify the traffic flow: estimate population → working adults → cars per minute
Identify when jams occur: morning rush (7–9am) and evening rush (4–6pm)
Generate creative low-cost solutions to reduce cars on the bridge or smooth traffic flow

questions.prompt: Estimate how many cars cross the bridge per minute during rush hour.
questions.guidance: Strong answer walks through: total population 10,000 → remove ~20% children = 8,000 adults → apply 45/55 gender split → 3,600 men → spread over 2-hour rush window → cars per minute. Candidate should state assumptions clearly.

math.setup: Population 10,000; 20% are children so 8,000 adults; 45% are men so 3,600 men; all cross within a 2-hour window (7–9am).
steps: If each drives one car: 30 cars per minute
math.answer: Approximately 30 cars per minute cross the bridge during rush hour.

questions.prompt: What creative, low-cost solutions would you recommend to the mayor to reduce bridge congestion?
questions.guidance: Interviewer is looking for creative and varied solutions beyond generic suggestions. Strong answers include at least 3–4 ideas across different categories (demand management, infrastructure use, incentives, regulation). The standout answer references license-plate-based day restrictions (as used in Santiago de Chile to reduce smog).

brainstorming.prompt: Please be as creative as possible. What suggestions do you have to solve the traffic jam dilemma?

categories.name: Car-pooling / demand reduction
ideas: Give incentives to men who car-pool
Build car-pooling meeting points near residential areas
If 3 men car-pool, cars drop from 1,800/hour to 600/hour (30/min to 10/min)

categories.name: Bridge capacity optimization
ideas: Open both lanes to westbound traffic during morning rush (7–9am)
Open both lanes to eastbound traffic during evening rush (4–6pm)
This doubles effective capacity without building anything new

categories.name: Alternative transport incentives
ideas: Subsidize commuters who walk, use motor scooters, or bicycles
Provide secure bicycle parking at the factory

categories.name: Regulatory / demand-spreading measures
ideas: Assign workers color-coded license plates restricting driving to alternate days (e.g., red plates on Mon/Wed/Fri, green plates on Tue/Thu/Sat) — modeled on Santiago de Chile smog policy
Stagger shift start times further apart to spread peak load
Offer flexible working hours so not all workers arrive/leave simultaneously

recommendation: Implement a combination of car-pooling incentives and lane-reversal during rush hours as immediate low-cost measures
Consider a license-plate day-restriction scheme for a more structural demand reduction without capital expenditure
risks: Car-pooling relies on voluntary behavior change; uptake may be low without meaningful incentives
Lane reversal requires signage and enforcement to avoid head-on incidents
License-plate restrictions may be politically unpopular with workers
next_steps: Survey workers to gauge car-pooling interest and optimal meeting-point locations
Pilot contraflow lane during one rush-hour period and measure queue length
Consult with local government on feasibility of day-restriction regulation
